Saved snapshot: 2026-11-02T21:18:15.574698+00:00. This page shows recorded progress, not a live cluster monitor; all 105 questions remain in the planned evaluation.

Native time sweeps

Each model receives the same 123 waveforms as the revised DuplexOmni study: the request alone, then progressively earlier sentences, for headset mix, one distant microphone and the beamformed microphone array. All histories end at the same question. DuplexOmni’s rows reuse its earlier native fields, including three generation failures; the other two models were newly run. The answer window is 19.2 seconds of input time; this is an accuracy diagnostic, not a latency test.

Table 1. Completed means the input was fully processed; nonempty means at least one non-whitespace text character, not a correct or meaningful answer.Scroll sideways on a narrow screen.

ModelCompleted / 123FailedNonempty native text / 123Source-complete / 33
DuplexOmni120/1233120/1230/33
Moshi123/1230119/1230/33
MiniCPM123/1230123/1230/33

Only the last eleven history lengths contain the complete supporting exchange, giving 33 eligible recordings per model. Codex reviewed these native strings against the source: C reported putting the files in the shared folder, D initially saw only their own presentation, and successful access was not verified. Shorter histories are excluded from complete-answer accuracy. These are one-question development counts, not full-bank results. Per-answer source decisions and evidence

Download every native string (CSV) · Native strings, exact history lengths and output-window definitions (JSON)

DuplexOmni listens under constrained decoding and starts answering at the known question end. Moshi and MiniCPM keep their native speaking decisions and generated state. Their 80 ms and 1 s frames differ from DuplexOmni’s 480 ms frames; full request-onward text and the matched post-input window are both retained. These caller differences limit causal comparisons between model architectures.

Generated speaker-attributed transcripts

  • Decode only audio available before each shared chunk boundary or user request.
  • Run Parakeet TDT or Whisper-large-v3 for words, with the same four-speaker Sortformer diarizer for speaker boundaries.
  • Use generated word times to assign words to predicted speakers; align Whisper’s recognized words back to the same audio because its native times drifted into silence.
  • Compare automatic requester-voice matching with annotation-based A–D naming, while retaining exactly the same predicted words and boundaries.

Both methods produced 61 chunk/request transcripts over five meetings. Parakeet supplies native word times. Whisper uses the existing Wav2Vec2 CTC aligner with recognized words only; no reference words enter alignment. All clips in the latest saved Whisper output passed the alignment procedure; this does not certify word correctness. Automatic voice matching identifies 5 requesters and leaves 1 unknown. Annotation-based naming uses only the source annotations available at that cutoff; it does not repair recognition errors, merged speakers or swapped turns.

A first greedy Whisper run repeated a thank-you sentence many times in one segment. The final inputs use predicted speech regions plus Whisper’s native temperature fallback, repetition, log-probability and silence checks; original outputs remain preserved. Alignment follows recognition and cannot repair invented words.

The fixed schedule comes from the original ground-truth pilot and is shared across transcript conditions; online boundary estimation is not tested. The six questions, thinking goals, note limits, reader prompts and decoding settings are unchanged. The question text is kept as ground truth to isolate errors in the earlier meeting history; request recognition is not tested here. Earlier notes finish before the worker opens the request file. These are past-only offline replays: actual ASR/note completion times have not been tested for real-time use. Sortformer was trained partly on AMI, so this is not an unseen-corpus test.

Matched-input and cutoff checks · Methods, model sources and unchanged reader settings · Prefix word-error diagnostics and normalization

Generated-transcript S2 runs

Each input variant runs Qwen3-30B Instruct and Thinking in separate vLLM processes. Per reader there are 104 earlier calls and 24 final answers: six questions in each of reactive reading, amortized summaries, structured notes and an extra source-excerpt diagnostic. Only the first three conditions are the main comparison. Each of the two note goals is queried at the same 52 boundaries.

Earlier results failing final-JSON or source-ID checks are excluded from saved notes; their generated tokens and GPU cost are still counted. These checks cover JSON completion, expected list/string fields and available source IDs, not factual correctness.

What a scorer disagreement means

The local automatic judge and an earlier Codex source review assigned different completeness labels to the same saved answer. They agree on 55/68 answers; the judge marks 11 additional answers complete and marks two earlier complete answers incomplete. Neither set is independent human ground truth, so disagreement calls for source inspection.

Assistant, what did we decide about capital letters when a sentence continues into the next segment?

Actual answer: When a sentence continues into the next segment, you do not capitalize the beginning of the next segment. This is only done when the sentence is clearly continuing from the previous one, and a hyphen may be used in such cases. Otherwise, capitalize as normal.

Earlier Codex label: partial. Automatic judge: complete.

The answer gets capitalization right but adds a hyphen for continuation; the later source says a hyphen is used when the sentence is definitely not continuing. The judge overlooks this unsupported extra rule.

Assistant, can we confirm when the detailed design phase begins relative to the others?

Actual answer: The meeting material does not specify when the detailed design phase begins relative to other phases. It only lists the detailed design phase as including product evaluation, following conceptual design and user requirements specification.

Earlier Codex label: partial. Automatic judge: complete.

The answer first says the relative timing is not specified, then says detailed design follows conceptual design and requirements. Codex flagged that contradiction; the judge credited the correct order without addressing the contradictory opening.

Assistant, what was the final decision on the slide panel's backlighting after the discussion?

Actual answer: The final decision was to include a backlight for the slide panel to light it up when opened, as it was considered fancy and usable. This was agreed upon despite initial uncertainty about reachability.

Earlier Codex label: complete. Automatic judge: partial.

This is the opposite direction: Codex accepted opening-triggered slide-panel backlighting, while the judge demanded an explicit interior-versus-buttons distinction and rejected extra rationale. Some source labels and optional-detail rules need review too; disagreement alone does not establish which rater is correct.

The capitalization example contains a correct main fact plus an incorrect extra rule; the judge accepted both. The backlight example shows the reverse issue: the judge demanded a detail Codex treated as optional. The scoring rules and earlier labels both need review. ASR means automatic speech recognition: the records here transcribe generated audio and may be empty, including for a failed replay. They do not establish correct answers. All three native allocations have finished. One DuplexOmni replay stopped before its question: on ES2002b, the ASR field repeated during listening at about 177 seconds and reached the 256-token generation limit. Moshi uses its native prompt interface; MiniCPM and DuplexOmni receive a fixed meeting-role instruction without question-specific facts. Native packet sizes are 80 ms, 1 s and 480 ms respectively. Every packet receives its normal model step; generated state is retained. DuplexOmni uses constrained listening and the known question end to start answering; the other models retain their native speaking decisions. These controlled accuracy runs do not measure conversational latency.

Up to 60 seconds of silent input follows each request, preserving the shorter 19.2-second comparison through recorded packet decisions. Final-packet speech and native end-of-turn information are inspected before fixing the full-study endpoint. AMI speaker letters are transcript labels, not spoken participant names; speaker-identification limits are kept distinct from recalling a fact.

What to think: first text comparison

The text models receive ground-truth speaker-attributed transcripts. Earlier calls use only the past transcript, previous saved results and a fixed goal; they finish before the worker opens the user-request file. Chunk boundaries use the first observed meaningful sentence end at or after 25 seconds, with a 40-second cap, satisfying the 10–40 second plan; sparse chunks do not trigger a model call.

Reference-answer validation

All 105 reference answers have Codex source reviews, with required facts, optional details and earlier evidence. The 382 supporting passages match the available transcript and end before their question. The shared evaluator accepts all 105 reference records. This is source inspection with earlier checks reused where recorded; independent human ratings have not been collected.

The automatic reference generator and checker produced 105 proposals and checks. They remain auxiliary evidence: some citations used times instead of segment IDs, and the checker also rejected supported facts. A separate input audit found that the earnings-call text loader omitted untimed words; the corrected loader preserves them until their next timed anchor. The twelve affected references were rerun, and the six AMI pilot inputs are unchanged.

Reviewed answers and source passages · Request, timing and evaluator checks · Frozen experiment design

Scorer qualification

The generic judge is tested on 68 earlier real answers to 17 questions from five meetings outside this audio pilot. Its prompt and thresholds were frozen before inference. It must complete every judgment, agree with the existing source-based pass/fail labels on at least 90%, falsely pass at most 5% of incomplete or wrong answers, and recover at least 85% of complete answers. These labels are earlier Codex reviews, not independent human ratings; the reader and judge also share a model family.

Current status: qualification failed. Recorded qualification results and disagreements. The full-bank comparison remains gated on this check and caller review; a weak but correctly executed S1 baseline is a valid result.

The generic judge did not qualify. All 68 judgments completed, but pass/fail agreement with existing source labels was 80.9%; 11 of 43 answers previously labeled incomplete or wrong were marked complete. Recall of previously complete answers was 92.0%. Review the disagreements and the earlier labels before changing the judge; these numbers do not establish an independent error rate.

What did the previous “WER cutoff” and “strict ASR criterion” mean?

The earlier diagnostic called a question recognized only when WER was at most 0.25 and the transcript also contained Assistant, shared, folder, conceptual and design. That extra keyword rule could reject an otherwise near-correct transcript because the wake word was missing. It was a diagnostic choice, not a standard definition of ASR quality. The current figures use continuous WER and omit that rule.

Figure 4: context-aware response quality

The local Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 judge receives the actual question, the source transcript corresponding to each selected audio suffix, a source-based reference limited to the evidence in that suffix, and the independent Parakeet transcript of the generated response. The source transcript is evaluation evidence; it was not supplied to S1. Microphone labels, context-length labels, S1 question-ASR results and earlier scores are hidden from the judge.

Topical relevance receives only the question and response. The model selects a response category mapped to a fixed rubric anchor: an offer without an answer is 3, a partial status report is 4, and a direct answer or explicit inability to determine the status is 5. Each dimension uses a separate judge call; adequacy also receives the factual-support assessment to check its use of available evidence. Topical relevance is not penalized by design for factual errors. A separate clause-classification call distinguishes factual assertions from greetings, offers and comments about missing evidence. Only factual assertions are scored for support against available source statements and the question, without the full reference. N/A is assigned when there are no such assertions. The judge gives separate 1–5 ratings, with higher values better. Question relevance asks whether the response addresses the question. Factual support checks material assertions against the available source evidence, and is N/A when the response makes no factual assertion. Unsupported means not established by this context; it need not be false outside the meeting. Answer adequacy asks how usefully and completely the response answers the question given its available context. A bare offer is not a completed answer; an honest inability to determine the status can be appropriate when the relevant context is absent. There is no combined score.

What the scores suggest

120 completed responses receive adequacy ratings of 1–2/5. 0/36 full-evidence responses reach the mostly-complete level (4/5). The answers are already poor across the tested lengths, so this run does not demonstrate a transition from reliably good to poor responses. Small differences between these low ordinal means do not establish a beamforming benefit or a reliable ranking of recording conditions.

Question-recognition WER averages for less than one minute, one to less than three minutes, and at least three minutes of earlier audio are Headset mix: 0.130, 0.706, 1.115; One distant microphone: 0.562, 0.737, 0.828; Eight-microphone beamformed audio: 0.630, 0.607, 1.000. The headset worsens on average, but individual curves reverse and microphone settings do not share one sharp cutoff. These length bins summarize the curves; they are not estimated change points.

Full question-status reference evidence first appears at 193.17 seconds of earlier audio. The full-evidence contexts retain the same relevant utterances at the same recording times: adding earlier history does not vary the delay after those facts. The longest context also adds 74.89 seconds of initial recording silence. At shorter lengths, an honest statement of insufficient context could be adequate. This changing evidence availability prevents interpreting the plot as a controlled memory-capacity threshold.

The observed failures include offers to check that never become an answer, unsupported claims about current folder access, and replies about another meeting topic. The beamformed colour/voice-control example can have source-supported content while receiving adequacy 1 because it does not answer the folder-status question. The recording reports past observations and cannot verify live folder access; no responding-assistant tools were used.

The 12 repeated evaluations reorder fields in the adequacy prompt and repeat relevance/support prompts unchanged. Maximum observed absolute rating difference: 1 on the 1–5 scale. Primary ratings are retained; these checks are not confidence intervals or independent question trials. Separate Codex source comparison flags 3 relevance ratings and 2 factual-support outputs for overrating or a likely omitted claim. Those scores remain unchanged and the flags are selected examples, not a human-labelled accuracy set.

The judge evaluates response ASR against a clean source transcript, the question and a context-specific reference; it does not hear input/output audio. ASR errors, the single Qwen-family judge, subjective anchors and the lack of independent human ratings limit interpretation. Passing structure/citation checks and development qualification does not establish that every rating is accurate.

Judge prompt, reference design, qualification and papers

References are scoped to the selected history: omitted facts are removed, and histories without the folder discussion receive an insufficient-context reference. Separate criterion prompts use explicit per-score anchors, a short evidence-based critique before each rating, and a source-based reference. It does not require exact reference wording, compulsory PowerPoint keywords, or unavailable facts. The full context also includes D’s later difficulty cutting and pasting into another folder; that does not prove an outage or a completed assistant lookup.

The design draws on G-Eval for explicit evaluation steps and separate aspects, MT-Bench’s LLM-as-a-judge study for reference-guided grading and bias checks, and Prometheus 2 for criterion-specific 1–5 anchors and feedback. This is a Qwen prompting adaptation, not a reproduction of G-Eval probability weighting or a Prometheus model.

Qualification uses twelve authored synthetic responses plus an empty-answer guard, declared before actual-case scoring. They cover correct paraphrases, offers, greetings, contradiction, invented checks, unrelated biography, reference leakage into empty context, and appropriate abstention. Twelve actual responses are rejudged with the question, context, reference and response fields reordered in the adequacy prompt. The relevance and support prompts repeat unchanged as controls. These are development checks used during prompt refinement, not held-out accuracy tests or independent human validation. Passing output-structure and citation checks does not establish that every rating is correct.

Question ASR: Assistant, what's the status of the shared folder after we couldn't find the conceptual design files?

Actual response ASR: Let me the folder status for you. The folder is still there, but the files are missing. I can help you create a new folder and upload the files if you have them.

Local judge: Question relevance: 4 / 5; Factual support: 2 / 5; Answer adequacy: 2 / 5

The source-based reference states that when no earlier folder-status evidence is available, a complete appropriate response must explicitly state that the folder status cannot be determined or confirmed from this context. It also clarifies that merely offering to check is not a completed answer (score 2), and inventing a status is inadequate (score 1).

Question relevance: The response directly addresses the question by reporting the folder's status (it is still there) and the missing files, which constitutes a status report. Although it includes an additional offer to create a new folder, this is a minor detour and does not detract from the core status information provided. Thus, it fits the 'partial_status_report_or_detour' category.

Factual support: The claim that 'the folder is still there, but the files are missing' is not supported by the available context. The only input is a question about the folder's status, with no response or confirmation provided. Therefore, there is no evidence to support or contradict the claim. Since the claim goes beyond the context and introduces a specific factual state not present in the source, it is unsupported.

Answer adequacy: S1 is a mere offer to check, which does not constitute a completed answer and is insufficient on its own. S2 fabricates a specific status (folder exists, files missing) without any supporting evidence from the available context, making it substantively wrong. S3 offers a solution but does not address the actual question about the folder's status. None of the sentences acknowledge the lack of available context or state that the status cannot be determined. However, the critical evidence rule allows a 5 if the response explicitly identifies the insufficiency of context and avoids inventing facts. Since no sentence in the candidate response does this, the answer fails to meet the standard for a complete, grounded response. The response contains unsupported claims and offers, but no acknowledgment of the lack of information.

unsupported: The folder is still there, but the files are missing. The available context only contains a question (Q) asking about the status of the shared folder after the conceptual design files were not found. There is no statement confirming the folder's existence or the absence of the files. The claim introduces a factual assertion about the folder's state and the files' absence, which is not supported by any explicit information in the source. No response or confirmation is provided, so the claim cannot be verified as true or false based on the context. Source IDs:

Question-transition measurements, noise-only controls and resources

Frame root-mean-square (RMS) level measures average signal amplitude in 20 ms windows. Decibels relative to full scale (dBFS) express that level relative to maximum digital amplitude; more negative values are quieter. The dotted line at zero seconds marks the end of original source audio and start of the insertion. The plot floors silence at −100 dBFS for display.

Earlier pilot questions rerun with revised audio

Two existing listening methods are repeated for P01 at 5:09 and P02 at 9:21 using their original native prompt, sampling and history policy. Decode and clear generates a native recognition field, then discards speech/action fields during listening. Constrained decoding prevents those fields during listening. Both retain their original controlled first response after the known question end. These pilot controls use temperature 0.8 and a 65,536-token context, so they are separate from the greedy 49,152-token pressure curves above. All acoustic changes are baked into the input, with no runtime question amplification.

Retired input method and earlier failures

Do not reuse the single-WAV shortcut as a native S1 baseline. It supplied the entire meeting and request in one call, skipping the intermediate 480 ms audio/response turns expected by the released caller, and failed to yield reliable native spoken answers.
